extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in probability and stochastic processes
extracted.subtask_description: Statements and sufficient conditions (hypotheses) for functional central limit theorems (Donsker-type results), martingale CLTs, stationary-sequence CLTs, and related invariance-principle results plus applications to empirical processes (Brownian bridge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Donsker's theorem (Theorem 8.1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the hypotheses of Theorem 8.1.2, S(n·)/sqrt(n) ⇒ B(·), i.e., the associated measures on C[0,1] converge weakly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the functional CLT: the linearly interpolated scaled random walk converges to Brownian motion in C[0,1]. The text uses this as a basis for corollaries via the continuous mapping theorem and invariance principle remarks (Erdös–Kac).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous mapping principle for functionals (Theorem 8.1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ψ : C[0,1] → R has the property that it is continuous P0-a.s. then ψ(S(n·)/sqrt(n)) ⇒ ψ(B(·)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to derive distributional limits of path-functionals (maxima, occupation times, hitting times) provided ψ is continuous almost surely under the Brownian measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity condition for path functionals (examples 8.1.6–8.1.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria when a mapping ψ(ω) (e.g., sup, last zero, occupation time) is continuous at a path ω: e.g., ψ(ω)=max ω(t) is continuous on C[0,1]; ψ(ω)=sup{t ≤1: ω(t)=0} is not continuous everywhere but is continuous at paths where the zero is not isolated; ψ(ω)=|{t: ω(t)>a}| is continuous at ω if |{t: ω(t)=a}|=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To apply Theorem 8.1.5, verify continuity P0-a.s. The text shows Brownian paths satisfy these continuity conditions with probability one (e.g., Fubini argument shows P0(|{t: Bt=a}|>0)=0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding/stopping-time closeness lemma (Lemma 8.1.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If τ^n_[ns] → s in probability for each s ∈ [0,1] then ||S_n,(n·) − B(·)|| → 0 in probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma reduces convergence of interpolated sums to showing that the constructed stopping-time sequence approximates deterministic time; used in proofs via Skorokhod/embedding constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence of expectations for bounded continuous functionals (Lemma 8.1.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ is bounded and continuous then E φ(S_n,(n·)) → E φ(B(·)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from tightness/metric convergence (Lemma 8.1.9) and the usual bounded-continuous mapping results; used to conclude weak convergence in C[0,1].

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension to C[0,∞) (Theorem 8.1.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: S(n·)/sqrt(n) ⇒ B(·) as measures on C[0,∞) (weak convergence on C[0,M] for every finite M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One proves weak convergence on every finite time interval [0,M] by the same arguments as on [0,1].

rubrics_metrics.name: Strassen embedding for martingales (Theorem 8.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S_k is a square-integrable martingale with S0=0, and B_t is Brownian motion, there exist stopping times 0 = T0 ≤ T1 ≤ ... such that (S0,...,Sk) d= (B(T0),...,B(Tk)) for all k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructs an exact finite-dimensional coupling of a martingale with Brownian motion via conditional distributions and the strong Markov property; used to transfer limit results to martingale arrays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Almost-sure convergence criterion for martingales (Theorem 8.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F_m = σ(S0,...,Sm) and sum_{m=1}^∞ E((S_m − S_{m−1})^2 | F_{m−1}) < ∞, then lim_{n→∞} S_n exists and is finite a.s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses embedding and stopping time arguments; sums of conditional variances finite imply the martingale converges a.s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedman's functional CLT for martingale-difference arrays (Theorem 8.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a martingale-difference array {X_{n,m}, F_{n,m}}, if (i) for each t, V_{n,[nt]} = Σ_{1≤m≤[nt]} E(X_{n,m}^2 | F_{n,m−1}) → t in probability, and (ii) |X_{n,m}| ≤ ε_n √n for all m with ε_n → 0, then S_n,(n·) ⇒ B(·).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condition (i) is conditional-variance convergence controlling quadratic variation; (ii) is a uniform negligibility/truncation condition to control large jumps. Proof via embedding and L2 estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lindeberg–Feller theorem for martingales (Theorem 8.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If {X_{n,m}} is a martingale-difference array and (i) V_{n,[nt]} → t in probability for all t ∈ [0,1], and (ii) for all ε>0, Σ_{m≤n} E(X_{n,m}^2 1(|X_{n,m}|>ε) | F_{n,m−1}) → 0 in probability, then S_n,(n·) ⇒ B(·).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lindeberg-type conditional second-moment vanishing replaces the boundedness assumption in Freedman's theorem; proof uses truncation, martingale orthogonality and error control lemmas (Lemmas 8.2.5–8.2.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Martingale central limit theorem for a single sequence (Theorem 8.2.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a martingale-difference sequence X_n adapted to F_n, let V_k = Σ_{1≤m≤k} E(X_m^2 | F_{m−1}). If (i) V_k/k → σ^2 > 0 in probability and (ii) n^{−1} Σ_{m≤n} E(X_m^2 1(|X_m|>ε√n) | F_{m−1}) → 0 for all ε>0, then S(n·)/√n ⇒ σ B(·).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the practical single-sequence martingale CLT used in applications; check conditional variance normalization and Lindeberg condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: CLT for ergodic stationary martingale differences (Theorem 8.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_n is an ergodic stationary sequence of square-integrable martingale differences with EX_n^2 = σ^2 < ∞, then S(n·)/√n ⇒ σ B(·).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ergodicity plus stationarity lets one apply the ergodic theorem to the conditional variances to verify the martingale CLT conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gordin decomposition CLT for stationary sequences (Theorem 8.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose X_n (n∈Z) is ergodic stationary with EX_n=0 and there is an increasing filtration F_n with θ^{−1}F_m = F_{m+1} and Σ_{n≥1} ||E(X_0 | F_{−n})||_2 < ∞. Then S(n·)/√n ⇒ σ B(·) where σ^2 = EX_0^2 + 2 Σ_{n≥1} EX_0 X_n (series absolutely convergent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decomposes X_0 = Y_0 + Z_0 − θ Z_0 with Y_0 a martingale-difference; the hypothesis (summability of conditional projections) is the key sufficient condition to reduce to the martingale case (Gordin's method).

rubrics_metrics.name: M-dependent and Markov chain special cases (Examples 8.3.3–8.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: M-dependent sequences (independence beyond lag M) satisfy E(X_0 | F_{−n}) = 0 for n > M so Theorem 8.3.2 applies. For irreducible aperiodic Markov chains on finite state space with bounded f, mixing properties yield the needed projection decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are concrete checks: for m-dependence the projection condition is trivial; for Markov chains one checks the n-step transition convergence to stationarity (total variation bounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: α-mixing covariance bound (Lemma 8.3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For σ-fields G,H and p,q,r ∈ (1,∞] with 1/p + 1/q + 1/r = 1, if X∈G, Y∈H have finite p- and q-moments, then |E(XY) − E(X)E(Y)| ≤ 8 ||X||_p ||Y||_q (α(G,H))^{1/r}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides quantitative control of covariances in terms of α-mixing; used to verify the projection summability conditions via bounds on ||E(X_0 | F_{−n})||_2 in mixing settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing sufficient condition for CLT (Theorem 8.3.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_n is ergodic stationary with EX_0 = 0, E|X_0|^{2+δ} < ∞, and Σ_{n=1}^∞ α(n)^{δ/(2+δ)} < ∞ where α(n) = α(F_{−n}, σ(X_0)), then S(n·)/√n ⇒ σ B(·) with σ^2 = EX_0^2 + 2 Σ_{n≥1} EX_0 X_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sufficient strong-mixing summability condition; the proof uses Lemma 8.3.6 with p=2+δ, q=2 to bound projection norms and apply Gordin's criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glivenko–Cantelli uniform convergence (Theorem 8.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For i.i.d. sample with distribution F, sup_x |F_n(x) − F(x)| → 0 almost surely (Glivenko–Cantelli theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets up the empirical-process context. For continuous F one reduces to uniforms and then applies Donsker-type functional limits to obtain finer (√n) fluctuation limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donsker limit for empirical sup (Theorem 8.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dn ≡ √n sup_{0<y<1} |G_n(y) − y| ⇒ max_{0≤t≤1} |B_t − t B_1| (the sup of a Brownian bridge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction via order-statistic representation and Donsker's theorem: the limit is the supremum norm of the Brownian bridge (Bt − t B1). Identification of the Brownian bridge distribution and techniques (conditioning or reflection principle) follow in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and density computations for the Brownian bridge (formulas (8.4.3) and Theorem 8.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The process {B_t − t B_1} (0≤t≤1) has the same finite-dimensional distributions as the Brownian motion conditioned on B_1=0 (the Brownian bridge). Theorem 8.4.4 provides an explicit infinite-series density for Bt on the event {T_a ∧ T_b > t} using reflections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These identities justify identification of the empirical-process limit and allow computation of tail probabilities/distribution of sup |bridge| via reflection-principle type series expansions.
